title: Strings: length, <string.h> and practice day 2
overview: Module 11 goes deeper into C strings. A string is a char array ending in the null character `'\0'`, and most string work is built on that one fact. You count a string's length by hand, then with `strlen`, and you meet the other `<string.h>` helpers: `strcpy`, `strcat` and `strcmp`. The practice day (11.5) then uses them on five judge problems: comparing words, joining strings, adding up digits, weaving two strings together and finding a hidden word. The solutions use only what the course has covered up to this module: loops, conditions, char arrays, `scanf`/`printf` and `<string.h>`.

concepts.explain: Every C string ends with a hidden `'\0'` character. Functions stop reading when they reach it, not when the array ends.
concepts.snippet: char s[10] = "abcd"; // stores a b c d \0 and 5 unused slots

concepts.explain: Loop until you hit `'\0'` and count the steps. This is what `strlen` does for you.
Found in `<string.h>`. It returns how many characters come before the first `'\0'`. Spaces and punctuation count too.
`strcpy(dst, src)` overwrites `dst` with `src`. `strcat(dst, src)` adds `src` to the end of `dst`. Either way, `dst` must be big enough to hold the result.
concepts.snippet: strcpy(b, a); // b now holds the same text as a

concepts.explain: `strcmp(x, y)` compares the strings letter by letter. It returns a negative number if `x` comes first in dictionary (lexicographic) order, 0 if the strings are equal, and a positive number if `x` comes later.
`'3'` is stored as its ASCII code 51, not as 3. The digits `'0'` to `'9'` come one after another in the table, so `c - '0'` gives the digit's value.
One index `i` can walk two strings at once. Guard every access with `i < length`, so the shorter string stops while the longer one continues.
concepts.snippet:
if(i < length_s) printf("%c", s[i]);
if(i < length_t) printf("%c", t[i]);

concepts.explain: A subsequence keeps the order but may skip letters. To see if `"hello"` hides inside `S`, walk `S` once and move to the next wanted letter whenever you meet the current one.

files.title: String length with a loop
files.what: Counts the characters in `"abcd"` without any library function. The loop walks the array until it reaches the null terminator.
steps: `char str[10] = "abcd";` sets aside 10 slots but uses only 5: four letters and `'\0'`.
`length` starts at 0.
The `for` loop runs while `str[i] != '\0'`, so it visits indexes 0, 1, 2 and 3.
Each pass adds 1 to `length`. At index 4 the loop finds `'\0'` and stops.
`printf("%d", length)` prints the count.
files.output_note: It prints `4`: the number of letters, not the array size 10. There is no newline after it.
files.watch_out: Don't loop up to the array size (`i < 10`). The slots after `'\0'` are not part of the string.

check.q: What would this program print if the string were `"hi there"`?
check.a: 8, because the space counts as a character.

files.title: String length with strlen
files.what: Gets the same kind of answer with `strlen` from `<string.h>`. The string here has a space and a `?` in it, to show that every character counts.
steps: `#include <string.h>` makes `strlen` available.
`char str[10] = "abcd ab?";` holds 8 characters plus `'\0'`, so 9 of the 10 slots are used.
`strlen(str)` counts characters until the first `'\0'`.
The result goes into `length` and is printed.
files.output_note: It prints `8`: a, b, c, d, the space, a, b and `?`.
files.watch_out: If a string has `'\0'` in the middle (for example `"hi\0there"`), `strlen` stops at the first one and returns 2.

check.q: What is the longest string that fits in `char str[10]`?
check.a: 9 characters, because one slot must hold `'\0'`.

files.title: Compare: print the word that comes first
files.what: Reads two words and prints the one that comes first in dictionary order. `strcmp` does the whole comparison, so the program is one `if`.
steps: Read both words with `scanf("%s %s", x, y)`. Each is at most 20 letters, so `char x[25]` is enough.
`strcmp(x, y)` compares letter by letter from the left and stops at the first difference.
It returns a negative number when `x` comes first, `0` when the words are equal and a positive number when `y` comes first.
`if(strcmp(x, y) <= 0)` prints `x`. The `=` part covers equal words, where the statement allows printing either one.
Otherwise `y` comes first, so print `y`.
files.complexity: Time O(|X| + |Y|) · Space O(1) beyond the two words
files.input_note: The example from the statement: two words.
files.output_note: `acm`. Both words start with `ac`. Then `m` meets `p`, and `m` comes first in the alphabet, so `acm` is the smaller word.
files.watch_out: Dictionary order is not length order. `strcmp("b", "abc")` is positive, so `abc` is printed even though it is longer. And when one word is the start of the other (`ab` and `a`), the shorter one comes first.

check.q: Which word does the program print for `ab a`, and why?
check.a: `a`. The first letters match, then `a` runs out. A word that is the start of another comes first, so `strcmp("ab", "a")` is positive.

files.title: Strings again, now with strlen, strcpy and strcat
files.what: The same problem as `6_strings.c` in Module 10, solved this time with `<string.h>`. `strlen` gives the lengths, and `strcpy` + `strcat` build `A + B` in a third array.
steps: Read `a` and `b`. Each is at most 10 characters, so `char a[15]` is enough.
`strlen(a)` and `strlen(b)` replace the two counting loops from Module 10. The results go into `int` variables and are printed on line 1.
`char joined[25]` must hold up to 20 characters plus `'\0'`.
`strcpy(joined, a)` copies `a` into it, then `strcat(joined, b)` adds `b` to the end. Printing `joined` gives line 2.
Line 3 swaps `a[0]` and `b[0]` through a temporary `char`, then prints both strings with a space between them.
files.input_note: The example from the statement: A on the first line, B on the second.
files.output_note: `4 2`, then `abcdef`, then `ebcd af`. On line 3 the first letters `a` and `e` have traded places.
files.watch_out: `strcat` does not check the size of its target. If `joined` were `char joined[15]`, two 10-letter strings would write past its end. Make the target big enough for both strings and the `'\0'`.

check.q: Why is `strcpy(joined, a)` needed before `strcat(joined, b)`?
check.a: `strcat` adds to whatever `joined` already holds, and a new array holds leftover junk with no `'\0'`. `strcpy` gives it a proper starting string.

files.title: Count: add up the digits of a long number
files.what: Reads a string of up to a million digits and prints the sum of the digits. The number is far too long for any integer type, so it is read as text and each character is turned into its value.
steps: `char s[1000005]` holds up to 10^6 digits plus `'\0'`.
`scanf("%s", s)` reads the digits as text.
`int length = strlen(s);` is worked out once, before the loop. Writing `i < strlen(s)` would walk the whole string again on every pass.
For each character, `s[i] - '0'` gives its value (`'5' - '0'` is 5), and that value is added to `sum`.
Print `sum`. The largest possible answer is 9 × 10^6 = 9,000,000, which fits in an `int`.
files.watch_out: Writing `sum = sum + s[i]` without `- '0'` adds the ASCII codes: for `351` you would get 51 + 53 + 49 = 153 instead of 9.

check.q: Why read the input as a string instead of with `scanf("%lld", ...)`?
check.a: It can have a million digits. Even `long long` holds only about 19 digits.

files.title: I Love strings: weave two strings together
files.what: For each test case prints the letters of S and T taken in turn: S0, T0, S1, T1, and so on. When one string runs out, the rest of the other one follows.
steps: Read the number of test cases `n`, then repeat the job `n` times.
Read `s` and `t`, and get their lengths with `strlen`.
Find `longer`, the bigger of the two lengths, with one `if`.
Loop `i` from `0` to `longer - 1`. Print `s[i]` only when `i < length_s`, then `t[i]` only when `i < length_t`.
Once the shorter string is used up, its `if` stops firing and only the longer string keeps printing. That adds its leftover letters at the end without a separate loop.
Print `\n` after each test case.
files.complexity: Time O(|S| + |T|) per test · Space O(1) beyond the strings
files.input_note: The example from the statement: 2 test cases, each with two strings on one line.
files.output_note: `icpcAssiut`: i+c, p+c, A+s, s+i, u+t. `egypt`: e+g, y+p, and then `t` is left over from the longer string.
files.watch_out: Without the `i < length` checks, the loop would read past the end of the shorter string and print its `'\0'` and whatever junk follows it.

check.q: What does the program print for `S = ab` and `T = xyz`?
check.a: `axbyz`: a, x, b, y, and then the leftover `z`.

files.title: Subsequence String: is "hello" hidden inside?
files.what: Prints YES when you can delete some letters of S and be left with `hello`, otherwise NO. One pass over S is enough: look for `h`, then for `e` after it, then `l`, `l` and `o`.
steps: Read `s` (up to 10^4 letters) and set up `char target[10] = "hello"`.
`j` is the position in `target` of the letter we still need. It starts at 0, meaning we are looking for `h`.
Walk `s` from left to right. When `s[i] == target[j]`, that letter is found, so `j++` moves on to the next one.
The check `j < 5` stops the program from comparing past the end of `hello` once all five letters are found.
Taking the first match every time is safe: it leaves as much of S as possible for the letters still needed.
At the end, `j == 5` means all of h, e, l, l, o were found in order, so print YES, otherwise NO.
files.input_note: The first example. The second example, `hlelo`, prints `NO`.
files.output_note: `YES`. The program uses the first `h`, the `e` after it, two of the `l`s and then an `o`.
files.watch_out: The two `l`s must be two different letters of S. Because `j` moves forward after each match, one `l` in S can never be counted twice, so `helo` correctly gives NO.

check.q: Why does `hlelo` give NO even though it contains every letter of `hello`?
check.a: The order is wrong. After `h` and `e`, only one `l` is left before the `o`, so `j` stops at 4.

recap: A C string is a char array that ends with `'\0'`.
The length is the number of characters before `'\0'`, including spaces.
`strcmp` returns a negative number, zero or a positive number depending on dictionary order.
Always leave one extra slot for the terminator, and make a `strcat` target big enough for both strings.
`c - '0'` turns a digit character into its value.
Call `strlen` once before a loop, not in the loop condition.

check_yourself.q: Which comes first in dictionary order, `apples` or `apply`, and why?
check_yourself.a: `apples`. The first four letters match, and then `e` comes before `y`.

check_yourself.q: After `strcpy(b, a)`, what happened to the text that was in `b` before?
check_yourself.a: It is overwritten. `b` now holds a copy of `a`.

check_yourself.q: What is `'8' - '0'`, and what is `'8'` on its own as a number?
check_yourself.a: `'8' - '0'` is 8. On its own `'8'` is its ASCII code, 56.
`ace` is: delete `b` and `d`. `eca` is not, because the letters appear in the other order.

body: By the end of the last module you had written the same four lines three times: walk a word one character at a time, stop at the hidden `'\0'`, count the steps.

Module 11 says: you have done it by hand, here is the ready-made helper. Put `#include <string.h>` at the top of the file and those four lines become one, `int length = strlen(s);`. Below is the walk `strlen` makes on the word `abcd`.
intro.trace:
s:   a     b     c     d    \0
i:   0     1     2     3     4
    +1    +1    +1    +1    stop

length is 4, and strlen(s) is 4 too

body: Nothing magic happened, so the rules you know still hold. Every character counts, spaces and punctuation included, so `strlen("abcd ab?")` is 8. It stops at the first `'\0'`, not at the end of the array, so `char str[10] = "abcd";` still gives 4.

One habit comes with it. `strlen` walks the whole string on every call, so work the length out once before a loop and use that variable inside. `for(int i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++)` re-walks the string on every pass, and with a million digits that is a million walks instead of one.

Three more helpers arrive with the same header, and each replaces a loop you could write yourself. `strcpy(dst, src)` copies a string into `dst`; you may want to write `dst = src`, but that does not compile for arrays. `strcat(dst, src)` sticks `src` onto the end of what `dst` already holds. Both write the closing `'\0'` for you.

Two things follow. `strcat` starts writing where the current `'\0'` sits, so the target must already hold a proper string; on a fresh array full of junk that is why `strcpy` comes first. And nothing checks sizes, so `joined` must be big enough for both words plus the slot for the terminator.

The most useful of the four is `strcmp`, because it answers a question you could not ask before. Two numbers are compared with `x < y`. Two words cannot be: `x < y` on char arrays compares where the arrays sit in memory, not the letters inside them.

`strcmp(x, y)` does what a dictionary does. It looks at the first letters; if they are equal it looks at the second, and so on, and the first difference decides everything after it. Here it is on `acm` and `acpc`.

A negative result means the first word comes earlier, `0` means they are identical, and a positive result means it comes later. Only the sign matters. Two cases are worth remembering: when one word is the start of the other the shorter one comes first, so `strcmp("ab", "a")` is positive; and dictionary order is not length order, so `strcmp("b", "abc")` is positive too.
intro.trace:
position    0     1     2
x = acm     a     c     m
y = acpc    a     c     p
            =     =    m < p   decided here

strcmp(x, y) is negative, so acm comes first

body: One more small fact comes back in the practice problems: a digit read as text is not a number. `'3'` is stored as its ASCII code, 51. The digits sit next to each other in the table, so `s[i] - '0'` gives the value. That is how a number with a million digits, far too long for any `long long`, can still have its digits added up: read it as a string and walk it.

Why bother with the header? Each helper is a loop you no longer write and no longer get wrong, so the length, the copy, the join and the comparison are one line each. The cost is that none of them checks that your array is big enough, which is now your job.

The five practice problems below use exactly these: `strcmp` to print the word that comes first, `strlen` with `strcpy` and `strcat` to report and join two words, `- '0'` to add up digits, and two lengths side by side to weave two words together or to find `hello` hidden inside a longer string.
